title: Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru v. State of Kerala
text: The basic structure doctrine is the bedrock of constitutional jurisprudence in India. Parliament's amending power under Article 368 of the Constitution of India is not unlimited and cannot be exercised to emasculate or alter the basic structure or essential features of the Constitution. Judicial review is a basic feature. Fundamental rights under Article 14, Article 19, and Article 21 form part of the constitutional scheme. (1973) 4 SCC 225, AIR 1973 SC 1461.
ratio_summary: Parliament cannot alter the basic structure of the Constitution under Article 368.

title: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
text: Procedure established by law under Article 21 of the Constitution of India must be just, fair, and reasonable, not arbitrary, fanciful or oppressive. The right to travel abroad is part of personal liberty under Article 21. Articles 14, 19, and 21 form a golden triangle and are not mutually exclusive water-tight compartments. Natural justice and audi alteram partem must be read into administrative actions affecting liberty. Citing Kesavananda Bharati (1973) 4 SCC 225. AIR 1978 SC 597, (1978) 1 SCC 248.
ratio_summary: Article 21 requires substantive due process: procedure must be just, fair, and reasonable.

title: Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab
text: The constitutional validity of the death penalty for murder under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code read with Section 354(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure is upheld. The extreme penalty of death can be inflicted only in the 'rarest of rare cases' when the alternative option of life imprisonment is unquestionably foreclosed. The court must balance aggravating and mitigating circumstances of both the crime and the criminal. (1980) 2 SCC 684, AIR 1980 SC 898.
ratio_summary: Capital punishment limited to rarest of rare cases with mitigating-aggravating balance.

title: Machhi Singh and Others v. State of Punjab
text: Applying the rarest of rare doctrine enunciated in Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab (1980) 2 SCC 684. Guidelines laid down for awarding death penalty under Section 302 IPC. Considerations include manner of commission of murder, motive, anti-social nature of crime, magnitude of crime, and personality of victim. Life imprisonment is the rule and capital sentence is an exception. (1983) 3 SCC 470, AIR 1983 SC 957.
ratio_summary: Formulated five-point guidelines expanding the Bachan Singh rarest of rare sentencing framework.

title: M.C. Mehta and Another v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak Case)
text: Principle of absolute liability laid down for hazardous and inherently dangerous industrial activities. The enterprise owes an absolute and non-delegable duty to the community to ensure no harm results. The rule in Rylands v. Fletcher with its exceptions does not apply in India. Article 32 of the Constitution empowers the court to award compensation for violation of fundamental rights under Article 21. (1987) 1 SCC 395, AIR 1987 SC 1086.
ratio_summary: Absolute liability for hazardous industries without Rylands v Fletcher exceptions.

title: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India
text: Sustainable development, Precautionary Principle, and Polluter Pays Principle are essential features of Indian environmental law derived from Article 21 of the Constitution of India. Remediation of damaged environment and compensation to victims are part of the liability of polluting tanneries. Citing M.C. Mehta Oleum Gas case (1987) 1 SCC 395. (1996) 5 SCC 647, AIR 1996 SC 2715.
ratio_summary: Precautionary principle and polluter pays principle integrated into Article 21.

title: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) and Another v. Union of India
text: The right to privacy is a fundamental right protected under Article 21 and the entirety of Part III of the Constitution of India. Informational privacy, bodily autonomy, and spatial privacy are core aspects. Any invasion of privacy must satisfy the three-fold test of legality, legitimate state aim, and proportionality. Overruling MP Sharma and Kharak Singh to the extent they held privacy is not a fundamental right. Reaffirming Maneka Gandhi (1978) 1 SCC 248 and Kesavananda Bharati (1973) 4 SCC 225. (2017) 10 SCC 1.
ratio_summary: Right to privacy is an intrinsic part of the right to life and liberty under Article 21.

title: Navtej Singh Johar and Others v. Union of India
text: Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code, insofar as it criminalizes consensual sexual acts between adults in private, is unconstitutional as it violates Article 14, Article 15, Article 19, and Article 21 of the Constitution of India. Constitutional morality trumps majoritarian popular morality. The right to personal autonomy, dignity, and choice of identity are protected under the privacy doctrine. Citing Puttaswamy (2017) 10 SCC 1 and Maneka Gandhi. (2018) 10 SCC 1, AIR 2018 SC 4321.
ratio_summary: Consensual adult sexual conduct decriminalized; Section 377 IPC declared unconstitutional in part.

title: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India
text: Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 is struck down in its entirety as being violative of the freedom of speech and expression guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution of India. The provision suffers from the vice of vagueness and overbreadth, creating a chilling effect on speech. Discussion, advocacy, and incitement distinguished. Clear and present danger standard examined. (2015) 5 SCC 1, AIR 2015 SC 1523.
ratio_summary: Section 66A IT Act struck down for violating freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a).

title: Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India
text: Freedom of speech and expression and freedom to practice any profession over the medium of the internet is constitutionally protected under Article 19(1)(a) and Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution of India. Any restriction or suspension of internet services under Section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure must pass the test of necessity and proportionality. Indefinite suspension is impermissible. Citing Shreya Singhal (2015) 5 SCC 1 and Puttaswamy (2017) 10 SCC 1. (2020) 3 SCC 637.
ratio_summary: Internet access is protected under Article 19; suspension orders must be proportional and published.
